text.p: The National Coffee Growers' Federation looks set to continue dominating Colombia's coffee industry for the foreseeable future. But there are growing signs of discontent with its authoritarian-style rule, which has been uninterrupted since 1927.

The federation marked its 70th anniversary with pomp and circumstance last week in the northwest city of Medellin, spending what observers calculated to be a small fortune on food, lodging, entertainment and transportation for hundreds of guests flown in from Bogota.

But amid all the lavish praise heaped on the organization there were some who marked the event with calls for change in the way it has run Colombia's coffee industry almost single- handedly for as long as the Institutional Revolutionary Party has held a stranglehold on politics in Mexico.

Among speakers at the ceremony the most vocal critic of the federation was Mario Corti, chief financial officer of Nestle AG who questioned both the "intrinsic quality of Colombian coffee" and the effectiveness of the federation's production policies.

On the sidelines, meanwhile, coffee growers said the federation's self-congratulatory "birthday party" flew in the face of debt-strapped farmers and the scarce resources available to support an industry that was once the mainstay of Colombia's economy.

Corti, speaking for the consumer side of the trade, referred in his closely-watched speech to problems that have a direct bearing on the future of Colombia's coffee industry. Among these he stressed "broca" -- or the berry borer now infecting at least 70 percent of Colombia's coffee farms -- and resulting "off-flavors" in the country's beans which he said had never been satisfactorily explained.
Corti said Nestle had established a pre-shipment quality control office in Colombia early this decade to screen and approve the coffee exported to its offices around the globe.

But he said that while the rejection rate had dropped from a high of 24 percent in 1992 to a current 12 percent, less credit may go to the federation's broca-fighting skills than other factors. "These figures do not necessarily reflect an overall improvement in the quality of Colombian coffee," Corti said.

Corti also lambasted Colombian production levels, which have had an undisputed influence on this year's price volatility. He pointed to the fact that, since 1991/92, there had been no overall increase in output of mild arabica coffees while consumption had grown by seven percent during the same time period.
He added that he hoped the current, disappointing coffee year in Colombia had "marked the turning point in your production trend."

In a tacit reference to the World Bank's call for a global disbanding of coffee control boards like the federation, Corti also urged the government to adopt "market oriented sales strategies" and establish a "transparent (coffee export) registration system."

Even Medellin's conservative El Colombiano newspaper gave voice, meanwhile, to a statement from the local Antioquia Coffee Producers' Association (APROCAFE) slamming what it described as "wasteful spending" on partygoing while many of the country's growers were suffering under the burden of debt and sky-high interest rates demanded by the federation-controlled Bancafe bank. The statement also criticized recent cuts in federation- controlled internal coffee prices paid to growers.

"The federation is interested in anything but coffee growers," Pablo Edgar Gomez, APROCAFE's chief legal representative told Reuters, saying it policies had done little but enrich its executives while growers faced a growing wave of bankruptcies and foreclosures on their farms.
"If the country is corrupt the federation is worse," Gomez said.

The general tone of his remarks were echoed in a letter this week to President Ernesto Samper from the Unidad Cafetera Nacional, a loosely-woven pressure group of coffee growers with a presence in nine provinces.

There had been no bonanza for Colombian growers despite the recent run up in world coffee prices, the letter said, adding that this was because the federation's misguided policies had driven many farmers to ruin.
